cues.text:
You fall into Jupiter at
210,000 kilometers an hour,
and there is no ground to stop you.
So where do you actually stop?
Here are the rules.

You start at rest, 1,000,000 kilometers
from Jupiter's center, and you let go.
No rocket, no parachute. Only gravity.
At first, nothing seems to happen.

Jupiter is a striped
coin hanging in the dark.

But it is pulling, and
the pull never lets go.

For 27 hours you fall,
while Jupiter spins about

2.7 times beneath you and
swells to fill the sky.

By the end you are moving
at 57 kilometers per second.

That is 57 times faster
than a rifle bullet,

and faster than NASA's Galileo probe,
which hit this atmosphere at 47.4.
For scale: Jupiter is 11 Earths wide.
The Great Red Spot alone, a storm,

is about twice as wide
as our whole planet.
And there is no ground.
Jupiter has no surface at all.

So on the way down we
will track three things:

how deep you are, how hot it is,
and what you see out the window.
Then the air arrives, and not gently.

At 57 kilometers per second even
thin hydrogen hits like a wall.

The gas ahead of you is
crushed into glowing plasma,
as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Every kilogram of you carries the
energy of about 390 kilograms of TNT.

For a whole person, that is about
28 tonnes, released in moments.

Galileo survived this behind a heat
shield and still felt more than 200 g.

The most any human has
survived on purpose is 46.2 g.
Galileo took more than four times that.
So honestly? You do not survive the entry.

You become a meteor, a streak
of light above the clouds.

But this is The If Engine,
so we cheat exactly once.

Put yourself in an indestructible
pod, your size and your weight.
Everything outside it stays real.

The pod slows to a fall
you could almost call calm:
about 690 kilometers an hour.

The thicker the air, the slower you
fall, and from here it only gets thicker.
First rung.

Depth: just above the 1 bar level,
Jupiter's version of sea level.
Temperature: about 120 degrees below zero.
Out the window: white.
These high white clouds are ammonia ice,

a snow made of the chemical
in household cleaner,
at about 0.70 bar.

The winds up here reach
539 kilometers an hour.
Here is the first surprise.

A study in 2025 suggests most
of the color you see from space

comes from deeper, from a
rust-colored layer below this one.
So let's go and look.
Second rung. Depth: about 18 kilometers.

Pressure: 2 bar, double the
air on a beach on Earth.
Temperature: about 72 degrees below zero.

These are crystals of
ammonium hydrosulfide,
stained by a haze the color of rust.
The sunlight is fading fast.

And somewhere below
you, something flashes.
Third rung.
About 49 kilometers down, 5 bar,
12 degrees below zero and rising.
These are water clouds.

Real water ice and droplets,
like the storms at home.
And they are electric.

NASA's Juno spacecraft found
lightning even higher up,
where it is 88 degrees below zero,

fed by slushy hailstones of ammonia and
water that scientists call mushballs.

All three cloud layers together
are only about 71 kilometers thick.

About 36 minutes after you
passed the 1 bar level,
you are already 100 kilometers down.

You have fallen through
Jupiter's entire weather.

Then the temperature
does something strange.
About 65 kilometers down, at 7.5 bar,

the air outside is a
comfortable 20 degrees Celsius.

When the Galileo probe
reached this level in 1995,
NASA logged it in its timeline:

room temperature, about
30 minutes after entry.

It is the most Earth-like
moment of the whole trip,

and you could not breathe
for a second of it.

There is no oxygen to breathe
here, only hydrogen and helium.
Galileo kept talking for 58 minutes.
It sank about 160 kilometers.
Then its signal stopped.

Within about 10 hours, NASA estimates,
the probe was completely vaporized.

No working instrument has ever
reported back from below this depth.

You keep sinking. Your pod
is indestructible, remember.

But from here, the question
is not whether you survive.
It is what is left of the sky.
Fourth rung. 1,000 kilometers down.
The sunlight is long gone.
Temperature: about 1,900 degrees Celsius.
Pressure: around 8,000 atmospheres.

At that temperature the hull of your
pod glows orange, like steel in a forge.

Down here, heat is the
only light there is.

It took you about 21
hours to sink this far,
and the gas is now so thick

that you are falling at 27 kilometers
an hour, the speed of a bicycle.

And somewhere around here, the line
between gas and liquid simply disappears.
There is no splash and no surface.

The hydrogen just gets
denser and denser until,

without any line you could point
to, it behaves like a liquid.

NASA calls it the largest
ocean in the solar system.

Fifth rung. Thousands of kilometers
deep, sinking slower every hour.

Jupiter's jet streams reach
down about 3,200 kilometers.
You are already below them.

And then, about 14,000
kilometers down, you stop.
Not because you hit anything.

The liquid around you is
now as dense as you are,

so you float, like a
swimmer who stopped kicking,

in a sea of hot, crushing hydrogen,
under about 2 million atmospheres.

That is the answer to the
question from the start.

Jupiter has no ground, so
what stops you is buoyancy.
In a simple model of Jupiter's interior,

you come to rest about 20
percent of the way to the center.
Getting here took about 78 days.

You crossed 1,000,000
kilometers of space in 27 hours,

then spent 78 days
sinking the last 14,000.

And below you, out of reach,
is the strangest layer.

NASA thinks that perhaps
halfway to the center,
hydrogen is squeezed so hard that it
turns into a liquid metal,

and its churning powers Jupiter's
enormous magnetic field.

Deeper still, NASA's Juno found
that the core is not a solid ball.

It is dilute, partly
dissolved, with no clear edge.

Even at the very bottom,
Jupiter refuses to have a floor.
So here is the twist.

You set out to fall into Jupiter,
and you never touched it.

No surface at the top,
no floor at the bottom.

Just a world that gets
thicker and thicker,

until it holds you,
suspended, in the dark.
And Jupiter is the gentle one.

Next, we visit every planet
and ask a simpler question:
how long could you survive on each one?
This was The If Engine.
Run the impossible. Do the math.
